articles.title: Evidence of vertical soil hydraulic heterogeneity regulating hydrothermal simulations in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands
articles.titleEn: Evidence of vertical soil hydraulic heterogeneity regulating hydrothermal simulations in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands
articles.abstract: Alpine wetlands on the Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau host vertically structured and highly contrasting pore systems that fundamentally shape land and atmosphere exchanges, yet their hydraulic expressions and process implications remain poorly quantified. This study provides the first process based and depth resolved characterization of these layered pore structures using soil physical analyses and laboratory evaporation experiments. The derived Clapp–Hornberger parameters reveal coherent hydraulic contrasts, with surface layers dominated by macropore connectivity and showing high θ s and K s and low b that promote rapid drainage and evaporation, mid layer domains with lower θ s and K s and larger b that enhance retention in finer pores, and deeper layers that act as stable and persistent storage reservoirs. These properties together generate a vertical regime of rapid near surface drainage, delayed mid layer release, and long lasting deep moisture storage. When implemented in Noah-MP, this hydraulic stratification systematically altered water and energy partitioning during wet and dry periods and showed that vertical hydraulic heterogeneity rather than a single layer parameterization governs the timing and magnitude of evaporation and heat fluxes. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence that pore scale structure regulates profile scale hydrothermal responses in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands and establish a physically grounded basis for representing vertically heterogeneous hydraulic processes in land surface models.

articles.title: TRAILS – a novel framework for time-height-resolved attribution of long-range transported wildfire smoke
articles.titleEn: TRAILS – a novel framework for time-height-resolved attribution of long-range transported wildfire smoke
articles.abstract: Accurately attributing long-range transported wildfire smoke to specific sources remains challenging, especially for elevated plumes. This study presents the TRAILS tool (Trajectory-based Identification of Lofted Smoke), which extends the automated air mass source attribution tool of Radenz et al. (2021) to provide time- and height-resolved identification of wildfire smoke. By integrating 10 d backward trajectories from FLEXPART with a multi-sensor satellite detection algorithm, we calculate a vertically resolved Smoke Occurrence Fraction (SOF), quantifying the likelihood of smoke influence based on air parcel residence time within smoke-affected regions. TRAILS identifies where and at what altitudes smoke is present, but does not automatically attributes these layers to specific fire sources. A key innovation is a new, statistically significant linear relationship between Ozone Mapping and Profiler Suite (OMPS) Ultraviolet Aerosol Index (UVAI) values and smoke plume height for fresh tropospheric smoke, derived from collocated OMPS and CALIOP observations. TRAILS was evaluated against ground-based measurements from the fluorescence lidar (MARTHA) and Raman lidar (Polly XT ) in Leipzig during the 2023 Canadian wildfire season. Results show that TRAILS effectively reproduces the vertical distribution and temporal evolution of long-range smoke layers, with a 76 % detection rate for fluorescent aerosol layers. Systematic underestimation of layer heights by 0.4 km, most pronounced in the UTLS, is consistent with unaccounted diabatic self-lofting in FLEXPART. While TRAILS performs well for the Northern Hemisphere smoke events studied here, its application to other wildfire regimes (e.g., Southern Hemisphere, different fuel types) may require recalibration of thresholds and carries additional uncertainties related to dust contamination. TRAILS provides a valuable, observationally constrained method for time-height-resolved smoke attribution, particularly where advanced fluorescence lidars are unavailable.

articles.title: A performance-based multivariable weighting framework for WRF parameterization-scheme selection
articles.titleEn: A performance-based multivariable weighting framework for WRF parameterization-scheme selection
articles.abstract: The selection of physical parameterization schemes is a major source of uncertainty in WRF simulations. A comprehensive evaluation of model performance requires the simultaneous consideration of multiple output variables, but simple multivariable averaging can dilute the influence of variables that are difficult to simulate or that respond strongly to alternative physical-process options. To address this issue, this study proposes a performance-based multivariable weighting framework for WRF parameterization-scheme evaluation. The framework combines two components: mean relative error, which represents variable-level simulation difficulty quantified by relative simulation error, and the coefficient of variation of absolute errors, which represents the scheme-dependent response of each variable within the evaluated physical-process group. The approach was applied and evaluated in assessing WRF parameterization schemes across two climatically distinct environments: the arid Northwest and the humid coastal Southeast of China. The results show that the method assigns greater weights to variables that are difficult to simulate, such as precipitation and 10 m wind, thereby helping identify physically interpretable and well-performing parameterization-scheme combinations under the prescribed evaluation framework. Compared with equal weighting and established statistical weighting methods, the proposed MRE × CV weighting helped identify parameterization-scheme combinations that achieved the lowest integrated cMIEI in both representative screening years and in the independent 2010 extreme-year validation. These results indicate that jointly considering variable-level simulation difficulty and scheme-dependent response improves the diagnostic relevance of multivariable WRF parameterization-scheme evaluation.

articles.title: Tracking recent extremes and interannual variability of global fire emissions using a near-real-time extension to the Global Fire Emissions Database
articles.titleEn: Tracking recent extremes and interannual variability of global fire emissions using a near-real-time extension to the Global Fire Emissions Database
articles.abstract: The Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED) is widely used to quantify spatiotemporal variability and long-term trends in burned area and fire emissions, supporting assessments of fire impacts on ecosystems and atmospheric composition. GFED has historically relied on observations from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), but orbital drift and planned sensor decommissioning pose challenges for maintaining record continuity and near-real-time (NRT) monitoring. Here we present the GFED5 near-real-time extension (GFED5NRT), a global fire emissions dataset that enables daily NRT analyses using active fire observations from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS). GFED5NRT uses biome- and region-specific lookup tables of effective fire area and fuel consumption, derived from VIIRS observations and standard GFED5 datasets, to estimate burned area and emissions from VIIRS active fire counts in a manner consistent with the GFED5 time series. Comparisons with GFED5 and independent datasets show strong agreement in spatial patterns, seasonal cycles, and interannual variability of fire activity. GFED5NRT captures recent major fire extremes and provides daily global NRT estimates of burned area and emissions for multiple trace gases and aerosols. Together, GFED5 and GFED5NRT provide a coherent framework for long-term analyses and NRT monitoring of evolving fire regimes in a changing climate. The GFED5NRT dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18702700 (Chen et al., 2026).

articles.title: A standardized permafrost ground temperature collection for Canada 2025
articles.titleEn: A standardized permafrost ground temperature collection for Canada 2025
articles.abstract: Ground temperature (GT) is an essential variable for monitoring the thermal state of permafrost, developing models, and conducting fundamental research. However, the usability of GT data in Canada is often hampered by inconsistent file formats, a lack of metadata standardization between organizations, and varied temporal resolutions. This fragmentation has prevented the development of a comprehensive benchmark dataset, leaving researchers reliant on small, ad-hoc data subsets for model evaluation. To address this gap, we present a new, standardized collection of GT and ground surface temperature (GST) data from across Canada, designed to serve as a benchmark for synthesis and model evaluation. The collection integrates data from 29 published datasets and 13 unpublished contributions, encompassing 427 GT and 491 GST sites across British Columbia, Labrador, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, Québec, and Yukon. The dataset includes records from 1960 through 2025 and observations range in depth from 0 to 300 m. The longest individual time series comprises 34 consecutive years of daily data with no more than 10 % missing data per year. On average for all sites and depths, this value is 6 years. All included time series feature at least one year of measurements at daily resolution. We performed quality control and standardization using tempcf – a newly-developed python software tool – to document and remove anomalies, outliers, and drilling disturbances. Then we aggregated sub-daily data to daily means. The dataset is standardized into NetCDF files adhering to CF, ACDD, and IOOS metadata standards as well as a compatible permafrost-specific metadata profile. Data are provided as both individual NetCDF files and text files. They are fully accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18022924 (version 0.9.1) (Meier-Legault et al., 2025) and via an ERDDAP server (https://data.permafrostnet.ca/erddap, last access: 21 July 2026), following FAIR principles. Several limitations remain, including time zone uncertainty in some datasets, and the lack of a standardized methodology for harmonizing site description metadata. Nevertheless, this collection improves the accessibility and usability of Canadian ground temperature data for national-scale permafrost research.

articles.title: The integrated benthic silicate flux in the Baltic Sea suggests a major land- or freshwater-derived reactive silicon source
articles.titleEn: The integrated benthic silicate flux in the Baltic Sea suggests a major land- or freshwater-derived reactive silicon source
articles.abstract: Coastal marine environments are hot spots in the global marine silicon (Si) cycle. Dissolved silicate (dSi) is an essential macronutrient for diatoms, which often dominate primary productivity in temporal coastal seas and constitute a key food source for grazers. Even though benthic release of dSi influences the ecology of coastal marine areas, direct rate measurements of dSi mobilisation remain scarce. The Baltic Sea is no exception, and the spatial coverage of benthic dSi flux data is low and limited largely only to regional reports. We report data from 305 individual measurements (mostly in situ) of benthic dSi fluxes conducted in different basins and sediment types of the Baltic Sea during 2001–2021. Using the benthic dSi flux data in combination with literature values, representative average fluxes for various sediment types in the major basins of the Baltic Sea were determined. An areal extrapolation using Geographical Information System (GIS) tools suggests an integrated annual benthic release of 8520 metric kilotonnes (kt) of dSi for the entire Baltic Sea. This benthic release of dSi is about ten times higher than the reported riverine transport of dSi to the Baltic Sea. Furthermore, this benthic load, together with the reported annual burial rate, is more than three times higher than the autochthonous export production of biogenic silica out of the photic zone. The integrated benthic dSi release being substantially larger than that cycled by diatoms may explain the trend of the increasing dSi standing stock in most of the Baltic Sea basins which has been observed since the 1990s. Overall, other major sources of reactive Si (estimated to be 6390 kt yr −1 ) to the sediment are suggested to exist, such as deposition of river and groundwater derived reactive (dissolvable) particulate amorphous and/or lithogenic Si. Our results strongly suggest that the biogeochemical Baltic Si cycle is more heavily influenced by reactive Si of terrestrial and freshwater origin than previously known.

Using the benthic dSi flux data in combination with literature values, representative average fluxes for various sediment types in the major basins of the Baltic Sea were determined. An areal extrapolation using Geographical Information System (GIS) tools suggests an integrated annual benthic release of 8520 metric kilotonnes (kt) of dSi for the entire Baltic Sea. This benthic release of dSi is about ten times higher than the reported riverine transport of dSi to the Baltic Sea. Furthermore, this benthic load, together with the reported annual burial rate, is more than three times higher than the autochthonous export production of biogenic silica out of the photic zone. The integrated benthic dSi release being substantially larger than that cycled by diatoms may explain the trend of the increasing dSi standing stock in most of the Baltic Sea basins which has been observed since the 1990s. Overall, other major sources of reactive Si (estimated to be 6390 kt yr −1 ) to the sediment are suggested to exist, such as deposition of river and groundwater derived reactive (dissolvable) particulate amorphous and/or lithogenic Si. Our results strongly suggest that the biogeochemical Baltic Si cycle is more heavily influenced by reactive Si of terrestrial and freshwater origin than previously known.

articles.title: Norway spruce shows stronger growth sensitivity and weaker intrinsic water-use efficiency response than Scots pine under increasing water limitation in southern Finland
articles.titleEn: Norway spruce shows stronger growth sensitivity and weaker intrinsic water-use efficiency response than Scots pine under increasing water limitation in southern Finland
articles.abstract: Boreal forests, essential for carbon sequestration and multiple ecosystem services, are increasingly threatened by climate-induced water stress. This study investigates how increasing water limitation affects growth and intrinsic water-use efficiency ( i WUE ) in Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris L.) and Norway spruce ( Picea abies (L.) Karst) in southern Finland from 1990 to 2022. Tree-ring data on basal area increment (BAI) and carbon isotope discrimination (Δ 13 C) were collected from three sites per species, with Scots pine on mineral soils and Norway spruce on organic soils and under contrasting soil moisture conditions. The tree-ring records were combined with regional growth indices (GIs) from the Finnish National Forest Inventory (NFI) to enable broader inference across soil types. Our results indicate that water limitation intensified over the past decade, with pronounced growth declines after 2016 in Norway spruce, while Scots pine exhibited smaller reductions, evident at the site level from around 2009 but not resolved in the regional GI. Δ 13 C analyses indicated increased stomatal regulation in Scots pine and more limited physiological adjustment in Norway spruce after 2016, consistent with rising atmospheric moisture demand. Accordingly, i WUE increased more strongly in Scots pine, whereas Norway spruce showed only modest changes despite a substantial growth decline. Interannual variability in growth and i WUE was related both to vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and to the summer water balance, but their relative importance differed between species: VPD had the larger effect per standard deviation in Scots pine, whereas Norway spruce responded to atmospheric demand and to the summer water balance to a similar degree. In Norway spruce, growth after 2016 was significantly constrained by VPD, whereas Scots pine showed comparatively buffered growth responses and stronger increases in i WUE . Soil-type effects were generally weak at the regional scale, but clearer patterns emerged along local moisture conditions. At the site level, both species tended to show greater negative post-change growth under drier conditions; however, Scots pine maintained higher mean growth on wetter sites, whereas Norway spruce showed higher mean growth under drier conditions. These contrasting growth–physiology responses indicate species-specific strategies in coping with increasing water limitation, with Norway spruce showing greater growth sensitivity and more limited physiological adjustment than Scots pine. Overall, boreal forest responses to drought appear to be structured primarily by species-specific physiological strategies, while being further modulated by local hydrological conditions. Accounting for both species differences and fine-scale variation in moisture availability will be critical for sustaining forest productivity and resilience under increasingly warm and water-limited climates in northern Europe, underscoring the need for site-adapted management that integrates species selection with local soil and moisture conditions.

articles.title: Areal reduction factors from high-resolution rain gauges in Austria
articles.titleEn: Areal reduction factors from high-resolution rain gauges in Austria
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Areal Reduction Factors (ARFs) are widely used to convert point design precipitation derived from intensity–duration–frequency (IDF) curves into areal precipitation values for hydrological design. Despite their importance, ARFs remain highly uncertain, particularly for short durations and small areas, due to insufficient representation of precipitation spatial variability. In this study, ARFs are empirically derived using a fixed-area approach for the Feldbach region in southeastern Austria using the WegenerNet, a dense rain gauge network with high temporal resolution (5 min) for the period 2007–2022. The results confirm that ARFs generally increase with duration and decrease with area, while pronounced dependencies on season and return period are observed, particularly for sub-hourly durations. Contrary to common assumptions, an application of ARF is required even for areas as small as 1 km 2 , indicating that point measurements and pixel-based precipitation estimates cannot be considered equivalent. For sub-hourly durations, ARFs increase partially with the return period. Seasonal analysis reveals smaller ARFs during spring and summer, associated with convective precipitation, and higher values during winter. The relationship between ARFs and topography is found to be weak, with only negligible correlations between ARFs and station elevation.

articles.title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
articles.titleEn: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
articles.abstract: Climate change mitigation reshapes the distribution of economic assets in the low-carbon transition. Here we quantify climate-related assets for 169 countries across four dimensions: fossil fuel production, climate change damages, renewable energy potential and land carbon sequestration capacity. We combine integrated assessment models, climate projections, economic damage functions and biosphere datasets to assess asset changes under multiple mitigation scenarios. Geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise from climate change mitigation because losses and gains across energy and environmental assets are country-specific, which we further characterize through a broad clustering and a detailed pairwise similarity analysis. Our analysis suggests comparatively moderate impacts for the USA, the European Union and China, highlighting the challenge that the largest economic powers may not be those with the strongest asset-based interest for climate action. While our framework remains limited, our data provide input for integrating other ethical, governance and socioeconomic factors in future analyses of opportunities and challenges for ambitious climate change mitigation.

articles.title: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
articles.titleEn: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
articles.abstract: Deforestation is a major source of global greenhouse gas emissions, and continued forest loss risks pushing the Amazon from a carbon sink to a carbon source. While recent work shows that productivity-led structural transformation towards less land-intensive sectors can reduce deforestation, the labour market implications of such pathways remain poorly understood. Here we address this gap by developing a spatially and occupationally explicit agent-based labour market model informed by empirically observed job-transition networks to simulate the ability of workers to respond to labour demand shocks. Our analysis reveals significant skill and geographic mobility frictions that constrain workers’ ability to adapt to structural change. Applying the model to productivity-driven development scenarios, we find that pathways delivering the largest deforestation and emission reductions disproportionately benefit high-skill workers while increasing unemployment among agricultural and other low-skill workers. Mobility-enhancing labour market policies can mitigate these effects, highlighting the importance of understanding labour market dynamics for equitable and feasible deforestation-reducing development pathways.

articles.title: Bridging Event‐Based and StorAge Selection Approaches to Backward Travel Time Distributions
articles.titleEn: Bridging Event‐Based and StorAge Selection Approaches to Backward Travel Time Distributions
articles.abstract: Event‐based backward travel time distributions (bTTDs) inferred from environmental tracer time series provide event‐scale insight into catchment transport, whereas StorAge Selection (SAS) functions describe integrated transport dynamics at the system scale. Despite their shared conceptual basis, their relationship across temporal scales remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a unified framework to directly compare event‐based and SAS‐derived bTTDs. Event‐based bTTDs are reconstructed from environmental tracer time series and expressed in event‐order space, while SAS‐based bTTDs are projected onto the same representation using storage‐age information. Building on this, we introduce a hybrid formulation that adaptively combines both sources of information. The framework is evaluated using controlled numerical experiments and a multi‐year field tracer data set. Event‐based bTTDs capture short‐term variability but are sensitive to noise and incomplete responses, whereas SAS‐based bTTDs provide smoother but temporally aggregated representations. In the numerical experiments, the hybrid approach consistently improves agreement with reference bTTDs, primarily through improved reconstruction of distributional shape while providing modest improvements in event‐order mean travel time estimates. Additional analyses of the numerical experiments indicate that increasing the complexity of SAS representations, such as through time‐varying formulations, does not necessarily improve hybrid reconstruction performance. Within the investigated model framework, stationary SAS functions provide the most robust basis for hybridization, suggesting that the SAS component primarily acts as a stabilizing system‐scale constraint. These results demonstrate that event‐based and SAS approaches encode complementary information and highlight the importance of balancing process detail and robustness when combining event‐scale and storage‐based transport models.

articles.title: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
articles.titleEn: Progressive oxidative weathering raised sub-arc mantle fugacity on the Archaean Earth
articles.abstract: In the modern Earth, sub-arc mantle oxygen fugacity is intrinsically associated with addition of sulfur species by slab fluids. However, it is unclear to what extent recycling of volatiles controlled redox changes of the sub-arc mantle in the early Earth. Here we use sulfur K-edge micro-X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy to measure the relative abundances of S 6+ , S 4+ and S 2− in apatite inclusions hosted by geochemically characterized and dated zircons from sub-arc sanukitoid magmas that span 3.4 billion years of Earth’s geological history. The sub-arc mantle shows marked increase in oxygen fugacity between 3.4 and 3.0 billion years ago (Ga). It is substantially more oxidized than unaltered ambient upper mantle, a characteristic that cannot be explained by fractionation, degassing or intrinsic mantle processes. We propose that progressive oxidative weathering enhanced the proportion of oxidized sulfur recycled to mantle wedge sources, establishing feedback between subduction of surface materials and incrementally oxidized arc magmatism. Early subduction involving inorganic oxidation and ‘whiffs’ of oxygen between 3.4 and 2.7 Ga may have regulated an early increase in fugacity of the sub-arc mantle before the Great Oxidation Event, matching similar conditions to the modern Earth by 2.1 Ga.

articles.title: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
articles.titleEn: Competing mechanisms toughen bcc binary and medium-entropy alloys at 20 K
articles.abstract: Plastic deformation in body-centred cubic (bcc) metals and alloys is conventionally mediated by screw dislocations. Their temperature-sensitive motion is attributed to a steep rise in strength with decreasing temperature that constricts plastic zones at crack tips, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition 1 . Here we evaluated the mechanical properties of group IV–V bcc refractory alloys with similar electronic structures at 20 K and found that these materials instead exhibit a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition. This behaviour arises from the global activation of twinning and an ω-phase transformation, which nucleate dislocations at interfaces before global dislocation motion. The initial mechanism is temperature insensitive and controls yielding, thereby preventing a crack-tip plastic zone from constricting with decreasing temperature.

articles.title: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
articles.titleEn: A microexon regulatory code reveals autism-linked genetic variation
articles.abstract: Neuronal microexons are a highly conserved class of alternative splicing events enriched in genes with critical functions in nervous system biology 1,2 . Microexon splicing is often disrupted in the brains of autistic individuals, and mice with microexon deficiencies display autism-like phenotypes 1,3,4 . However, the full landscape of microexons is not known, and the impact of genetic variation on these exons has not been systematically investigated. Here, through extensive transcriptome profiling, we detect hundreds of new microexons, including many with neuronal subtype-specific splicing patterns, and others that activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Using machine learning, we define a sequence code predictive of neuronally spliced microexons and use this to identify critical regulatory elements surrounding the expanded microexon repertoire. This code further reveals genomic variants predicted to alter microexon splicing in individuals affected by autism, with rare variants having the strongest estimated impact. These variants are mostly detected in idiopathic individuals and are associated with autism status. They also converge on synaptic and other autism-linked genes, as well as genes not previously linked to autism. Our results collectively define an expanded repertoire of microexons, delineate their regulatory code, and pinpoint variants predicted to affect their splicing, with implications for the disruption of functions central to neuronal biology and brain disorders.

articles.title: Characterisation and modelling of lightning strokes as point events in time and space
articles.titleEn: Characterisation and modelling of lightning strokes as point events in time and space
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Lightning is a spatio-temporal phenomenon comprised of individual strokes with specific occurrence times and spatial coordinates. This study models and characterises lightning strokes from single thunderstorms, treating each stroke as a point event. Utilising real-world datasets, we characterise and model lightning strokes' statistical properties. Our analysis involves two severe UK thunderstorm systems selected based on published synoptic analyses. These systems enable subdivision of the lightning dataset into subsets, each representing a distinct thunderstorm. Our two major storm systems feature three thunderstorms each: Storm system A with 7955, 11 988, and 5655 strokes over the English Midlands on 28 June 2012; Storm system B with 4218, 455, and 1926 strokes characterised over northern England on 1–2 July 2015. These six datasets exemplify individual thunderstorms, each characterised by three physical attributes: movement speed, lightning inter-event time distribution, and spatial spread about the storm track. Applying least-squares plane and linear fits in spatio-temporal and lag spaces, we estimate movement speeds of 13–17 m s −1 for Storm system A and 18–31 m s −1 for Storm system B. The inter-event time distribution ranges from 0.01 to 100 s, with density peaks around 0.2 and 1–10 s. Autocorrelation analysis in natural time reveals significant autocorrelation across all storms, varying from short-to long-range. For spatial spread, calculated as the distance from the storm track to the strokes, we employ a linear filter to establish the storm track. This analysis yields typical spatial spreads of up to 80 km in either northing or easting dimensions. The paper concludes with a synthetic lightning stroke model. This model allows the selection of each storm's starting points, directions, and movement speeds, generating point events based on our characterisation findings. This comprehensive study of lightning strokes in time and space provides a representative statistical description of severe thunderstorms' behaviour and informs statistical models for simulating lightning events.

articles.title: Reductions in Climate Zone Changes Under Stratospheric Aerosol Injection Compared to Unabated Warming
articles.titleEn: Reductions in Climate Zone Changes Under Stratospheric Aerosol Injection Compared to Unabated Warming
articles.abstract: As the goals of the Paris Agreement struggle to be met, interest in stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) has increased due to its potential to reduce the impacts of anthropogenic warming. SAI would aim to cool the Earth by injecting sulfate aerosols or their precursors into the stratosphere, reflecting incoming sunlight back to space. Previous work has shown that SAI could produce regionally varying temperature and precipitation impacts, however, along with global mean drying. Climate classification systems serve as a potentially useful tool in quantifying how concerning these impacts may be. We evaluate the effectiveness of SAI by identifying the types and magnitude of climate zone changes over time, which we term “adaptation burdens.” A modified version of the Köppen‐Trewartha climate classification system is used to identify changes in climate zones under a high greenhouse gas emissions scenario, a medium emissions scenario, and a scenario in which SAI is implemented such that global mean temperature follows that of the medium emissions scenario despite high greenhouse gas emissions. We find that changes in climate zones under this SAI scenario are similar in both magnitude and transition type to those under medium‐tier emissions, while shifts under high emissions are significantly greater in magnitude and diverge further from the historical baseline. While all models analyzed agree that SAI reduces adaptation burdens in comparison to a high emissions scenario, they disagree on magnitudes and regional distributions, indicating differing model responses to aerosol and greenhouse gas forcings.

articles.title: Assessment of an updated polar stratospheric cloud parameterisation for the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.1) within the UK Met Office Unified Model (v13.9) using CALIOP and MLS observations
articles.titleEn: Assessment of an updated polar stratospheric cloud parameterisation for the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.1) within the UK Met Office Unified Model (v13.9) using CALIOP and MLS observations
articles.abstract: Accurately representing polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) in global Chemistry-Climate Models and Earth System Models is important as they play a key role in springtime ozone depletion in polar regions by activating both chlorine and bromine species through heterogeneous reactions and denitrifying the stratosphere. Here, we present and evaluate an updated PSC parameterisation scheme implemented in the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.1). The scheme includes the kinetic formation of nitric acid trihydrate (NAT) particles, the formation of supercooled ternary solution (STS) droplets assuming thermodynamic equilibrium, and accounts for ice and sulphate aerosols. To evaluate the new scheme, we compare modelled PSC production with satellite observations from the Cloud-Aerosol and Lidar with Orthogonal Polarization (CALIOP) instrument and model concentrations of gas-phase nitric acid, water vapour, and ozone concentrations with observations from the Aura Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) instrument for the extended 2008 Antarctic and 2009/2010 Arctic winters. In comparison with the current, simpler scheme, the updated parameterisation increases both the range of PSC types that form and the seasonal variability, resulting in better agreement with CALIOP observations. However, there is still a gap in the model's ability to simulate ice PSCs with the full range of optical properties observed by CALIOP. The new scheme also slows the growth of NAT particles and enables nitric acid partitioning between gas, liquid, and solid phases, leading to improved agreement with gas-phase nitric acid MLS observations, although a substantial low-bias is still present in all model simulations. However, there is comparatively little impact on stratospheric ozone, with the exception near the edge of the polar vortex where the new scheme improves comparisons with MLS observations.

articles.title: High-performance geodynamics on GPUs using the PETSc CUDA backend (GAUZZ v1.0.0)
articles.titleEn: High-performance geodynamics on GPUs using the PETSc CUDA backend (GAUZZ v1.0.0)
articles.abstract: GPUs provide much higher memory bandwidth than CPUs. Data-parallel computations with regular memory access patterns exploit the GPU architecture efficiently. To solve the Stokes equations, we apply a preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PCG) method to the Schur complement system. The algorithm is dominated by sparse matrix-vector products, vector inner products, vector updates, and repeated velocity subproblem solves, all of which map onto GPU architectures. We implement the solver in GAUZZ v1.0.0 on GPUs by coupling CUDA-enabled PETSc with FEniCS. PETSc AIJCUSPARSE matrices with CUDA vectors keep operators and field vectors resident in VRAM, which limits CPU-GPU transfers. The P 1 mass matrix, the gradient operator, and the divergence operator are reused in the pressure-correction L 2 -projection step. HYPRE BoomerAMG was adopted for preconditioning the velocity-only subproblem. Accuracy and performance are evaluated on a manufactured solution, the SolCx benchmark, the sticky-air benchmark, 2D Rayleigh–Taylor instabilities, 3D thermo-mechanical convection, and a 2D subduction model with nonlinear viscosity. We confirm that the GPU-based implementation reproduces CPU solutions. Performance is quantified by the execution time of the pressure-correction step and by throughput, defined as the number of Stokes degrees of freedom divided by the execution time of one Stokes solve. A single GPU delivers 6–11× the throughput of a 32-core CPU across the Stokes benchmarks. Two GPUs increase the throughput at sufficiently large problem sizes, reaching up to 2.1× the single-GPU throughput. The two-GPU configuration also extends the maximum problem size to 2.5×10 7 DOFs, beyond the 48 GB VRAM limit of a single GPU.

articles.title: Enhancing the advection module performance in the EPICC-Model V1.6.0 via GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 coupling and GPU-optimized strategies
articles.titleEn: Enhancing the advection module performance in the EPICC-Model V1.6.0 via GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 coupling and GPU-optimized strategies
articles.abstract: The rapid development of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) has established new computational paradigms for enhancing air quality modeling efficiency. In this study, the heterogeneous-compute interface for portability (HIP) was implemented to parallel computing of the piecewise parabolic method (PPM) advection solver (HADVPPM) on China's domestic GPU-like accelerators (GPU-like), resulting in a GPU-accelerated version denoted as GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0. Computational performance was enhanced through three strategic optimizations: reducing the central processing unit (CPU) and GPU (CPU-GPU) data transfer frequency, thread-block coordinated indexing, and the Message Passing Interface (MPI) and HIP (“MPI+HIP”) hybrid parallelization across heterogeneous computing clusters. Following validation of the GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 program's offline computational consistency and the pollutant simulation performance of the Emission and atmospheric Processes Integrated and Coupled Community version 1.6.0 (EPICC-Model V1.6.0) on the Earth System Numerical Simulation Facility (EarthLab), comprehensive performance testing was conducted. Offline benchmark results demonstrated that, for a one-dimensional input array containing 10 8 double-precision floating-point values, GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 compiled with the −O3 optimization option achieved a maximum speedup of 556.5× on a GPU-like accelerator relative to the Fortran HADVPPM implementation compiled with the −O0 option as the baseline. Integrating GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 into EPICC-Model V1.6.0 yielded three distinct versions: the initial HIP-based version (HIP-Ori), a version optimized for CPU and GPU communication frequency (HIP-Opt1), and a further-optimized version employing a thread-block coordinated indexing strategy (HIP-Opt2). Compared to the HIP-Ori version, HIP-Opt1 achieved a model-level computational efficiency improvement of 17.0×. Building upon HIP-Opt1, HIP-Opt2 delivered an additional 1.5× enhancement in computational efficiency. At the module level, including CPU and GPU data transfer overhead, the GPU implementation improves computational efficiency of the advection module by 39.3 %; when communication cost is excluded, the advection module attains a 20.5× acceleration relative to its CPU counterpart. This coupling establishes a foundational framework for adapting air quality models to GPU-like architectures and identifies critical optimization pathways. Moreover, the methodology provides essential technical support for achieving full-model GPU implementation of the EPICC-Model, addressing both current computational constraints and future demands for high-resolution air quality simulations.

articles.title: Physics vs. AI in weather prediction: evaluating GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi against an observation-corrected WRF model for flash floods
articles.titleEn: Physics vs. AI in weather prediction: evaluating GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi against an observation-corrected WRF model for flash floods
articles.abstract: Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are increasingly positioned as alternatives or complements to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, yet systematic model evaluation studies that compare both paradigms under controlled experimental conditions remain limited. Here we present a structured model evaluation framework applying standardised verification metrics to assess a regional WRF configuration against three publicly available AI models – GraphCast, AIFS Single 1.0, and FuXi – over three high-impact flood events in Luxembourg and the Greater Region (2016, 2018, and 2021), comprising around 90 simulated days per configuration and 92 119 matched forecast–observation pairs at a four-country network of 259 to 280 stations per event, each screened to be independent of the observations assimilated in that event (Fig. 1). The WRF model employs a three-dimensional variational (3D-VAR) data assimilation scheme ingesting GNSS Zenith Total Delay and conventional observations on a 6-hourly Rapid Update Cycle. All systems draw their initial and boundary information from the same ERA5 reanalysis, although the effective initial states are not identical: WRF is cycled and, in the assimilated configuration, corrected by observations, and ERA5 lateral boundary forcing of a limited-area model differs structurally from a global rollout. Categorical precipitation scores evaluated at thresholds from 1 to 20 mm (6 h) −1 and continuous temperature metrics at surface stations serve as verification targets. Data assimilation raises WRF's categorical precipitation skill at the 1 mm threshold (Critical Success Index: 0.364 to 0.389, a difference not resolved by a block bootstrap over 24 h blocks) and brings the near-surface temperature bias close to zero, although this benefit does not extend to heavier rainfall: at 10 mm (6 h) −1 the assimilated run scores below the unassimilated one. The degradation appears in all three events and is not ordered by the density of the assimilated observing network, so we report it without attributing a cause. At the 1 mm threshold AIFS achieves the highest detection rate (POD 0.835) and GraphCast the highest net categorical skill (CSI 0.424, against 0.415 for AIFS and 0.389 for the assimilated WRF), and AIFS and GraphCast reduce temperature RMSE by 19.0 % and 17.6 % relative to assimilated WRF at the subset of stations that also report temperature. This ordering reverses as the rainfall threshold increases: at 20 mm (6 h) −1 WRF attains the highest skill (CSI 0.160), ahead of AIFS (0.141) and GraphCast (0.114), while FuXi produces no exceedances at all. A weather-radar comparison over 27 6 h periods shows the same reversal in space: AIFS holds the highest mean per-period Fractions Skill Score at 1 mm (6 h) −1 at every neighbourhood width, but at 20 mm (6 h) −1 both WRF configurations are ahead of all three AI models on that estimator, and a WRF configuration leads on the pooled aggregate as well. The per-event breakdown reveals no skill degradation for GraphCast on the 2021 event, which lies outside its training period – indeed its skill is highest there – demonstrating useful skill on this later event without identifying the cause of the event-to-event differences; the same test cannot be applied to AIFS, whose fine-tuning window encompasses all three events. These results provide a replicable model evaluation methodology for benchmarking emerging data-driven NWP systems against observation-corrected regional models.

articles.title: High-quality remote sensing reflectance products over China and US coast
articles.titleEn: High-quality remote sensing reflectance products over China and US coast
articles.abstract: Remote sensing reflectance ( R rs ) is fundamental for deriving bio-optical properties of global surface waters. However, accurate atmospheric correction (AC) to derive R rs in coastal waters remains challenging due to strongly absorbing aerosols and complex water optics. To address this, we developed an improved processing framework that integrates flexible use of global gridded aerosol models better suited for coastal environments and incorporates tailored masking strategies. Based on this framework, we generated a high-quality R rs dataset from Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Aqua observations, spanning 2003–2022 for the coastal waters of China and the United States (US) – two regions where complex water optics and frequent anthropogenic aerosols have long impeded retrieval accuracy and valid data yield. Compared to the NASA standard MODIS Aqua R rs products, the improved framework achieved a significant reduction in systematic bias. Multiple validation metrics support this, with the restoration of the mean regression slope to unity (1.00 ± 0.08 vs. 0.90 ± 0.06) across eight bands being the most prominent. Performance gains are particularly pronounced in the 488–555 nm range, which is most relevant to water color applications. The new dataset also yields significantly more valid retrievals, with regional mean increases of 56 % in the Chinese coastal waters and 18 % in the US coastal waters at 443 nm. Furthermore, it recovers fine-scale features in turbid waters and captures long-term dynamics, demonstrating its robustness for coastal monitoring. As a complementary resource optimized for estuaries, bays, and turbid coastal regions, the new dataset fills a critical gap in the ocean color data portfolio where standard products are less reliable. The dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16413443 (Zhao et al., 2025).

articles.title: Coastal Atmosphere & Sea Time Series (CoASTS) and Bio-Optical mapping of Marine optical Properties (BiOMaP): the hyperspectral absorption coefficients by optically significant constituents
articles.titleEn: Coastal Atmosphere & Sea Time Series (CoASTS) and Bio-Optical mapping of Marine optical Properties (BiOMaP): the hyperspectral absorption coefficients by optically significant constituents
articles.abstract: The Coastal Atmosphere & Sea Time Series (CoASTS) and the Bio-Optical mapping of Marine optical Properties (BiOMaP) programs were conceived and implemented to assist ocean color applications with field measurements of apparent and inherent optical properties, as well as concentration of optically significant water constituents. The CoASTS program led to the creation of time-series of bio-optical measurements at the “Acqua Alta” Oceanographic Tower (AAOT) site in the northern Adriatic Sea continued from 1995 up to 2016. The BiOMaP program supported the collection of equivalent bio-optical measurements across European Seas from 2000 up to 2022. This work focusses on CoASTS and BiOMaP hyperspectral absorption coefficients of optically significant constituents as determined applying standardized instruments, community measurement methods, extended quality control schemes and consolidated processing. The work, which complements a previous one by Zibordi and Berthon (2024) centred on multi-spectral data, presents the CoASTS and BiOMaP hyperspectral absorption coefficients of pigmented and non-pigmented particles in the 400–750 nm interval, and colored dissolved organic matter in the 350–680 nm one, both with a 3 nm spectral resolution at 2 nm increment. The data are available at https://doi.org/10.1594/PANGAEA.993510 (Berthon and Zibordi 2026).

articles.title: Temperate marine macrophytes are highly variable sources of Biogenic Volatile Organic Compounds – a comparative study from the Baltic Sea and NE Atlantic
articles.titleEn: Temperate marine macrophytes are highly variable sources of Biogenic Volatile Organic Compounds – a comparative study from the Baltic Sea and NE Atlantic
articles.abstract: Biogenic Volatile Organic Compounds (BVOC), emitted by Earth's ecosystems, affect several chemical processes in the atmosphere that have profound climate impacts. Despite their climate relevance, global BVOC budget estimations are still highly uncertain, with ocean-derived emissions being particularly poorly constrained. Marine macrophytes (i.e. macroalgae and seagrass) are a large and widespread organismal group whose BVOC emission rates are particularly poorly quantified. In this study, we set out to address this knowledge gap by quantifying ex situ the BVOC emission rates of three temperate macrophytes ( Zostera marina , Fucus vesiculosus and Ulva intestinalis ) with a Vocus proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Vocus PTR-TOF-MS). To capture and improve our understanding of the variability of macrophyte BVOC emissions, our quantifications were repeated across two contrasting coastal regions: the northeastern Atlantic (Ireland) and northern Baltic Sea (Finland). The three macrophytes emitted a wide range of BVOCs, with a total of 166 different compounds detected. Although many BVOCs were emitted by all macrophytes, significant differences were observed in the total emission profiles, both between and within species. Interestingly, the seagrass Zostera exhibited significantly higher overall BVOC emission rates per unit biomass than the two macroalgae and showed clearly differing intraspecific emission profiles across the two regions. Regarding individual compounds, dimethyl sulfide (DMS) was emitted at the highest rates, but many other compounds (e.g., sesquiterpenes and C 10 H 21 O + ) also displayed notable emission rates. Although many of the observed BVOCs are commonly investigated compounds (e.g., DMS and terpenoids), our results show that macrophyte BVOC emissions comprise a large number of different compounds, suggesting that future studies would benefit from targeting a wider range of BVOCs than currently considered. Our results highlight macrophytes as highly variable sources of BVOCs, whose better inclusion into marine BVOC budgets should be strived for. However, more robust data are needed, and future research should also focus on investigating the dynamics driving macrophyte BVOC emissions, their variability, and their eventual fate in the environment.

articles.title: The impact of the Canterbury earthquakes on household income and expenditure in the Canterbury region in New Zealand
articles.titleEn: The impact of the Canterbury earthquakes on household income and expenditure in the Canterbury region in New Zealand
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Using New Zealand's Integrated Data Infrastructure (IDI), we evaluate the effects of the 2010–2011 Canterbury earthquakes on household income and expenditure. We link data from the Household Economic Survey (HES) to administrative address histories and meshblock-level earthquake intensity, and implement a propensity-score-matched difference-in-differences (PSM-DiD) design comparing exposed Canterbury households with matched North Island households. We find that total and regular household income increase by approximately 7000–7900 New Zealand dollars (NZD) in both low- and high-intensity areas. Total expenditure shows no clear average DiD effect, but its composition changes substantially. In high-intensity areas, the magnitude of recorded receipts-and-refunds entries, an HES category that includes insurance reimbursements and related inflows, more than doubles, while spending on general insurance, transportation, telecommunications, diary-recorded day-to-day purchases, fees and subscriptions also increases. Expenditure responses are broader among above-median-income households than among below-median-income households. Households later observed outside Canterbury have housing costs around NZD 25 000 higher and mortgage and loan payments around NZD 9600 lower than households that remain, while conditional income differences are statistically insignificant. These findings show that post-disaster income growth can coexist with heterogeneous recovery costs and substantial changes in household expenditure.

articles.title: Multiscalar and nonlinear controls of drought impacts in Spain revealed by media-reported data

articles.title: Impact of Spatially Continuous Urban Surface Properties on Summertime and Heatwave Simulations: A Multi‐City Analysis
articles.titleEn: Impact of Spatially Continuous Urban Surface Properties on Summertime and Heatwave Simulations: A Multi‐City Analysis
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Urban areas are unique in form, function, and fabric, and representing them in process‐based models requires, among other things, prescribing facet‐level morphological and radiative properties, which vary widely. Most urban canopy models (UCMs) prescribe these by density class or local climate zone (LCZ), assigning identical values across broad regions or worldwide. Global km‐scale, facet‐level urban property data sets have recently emerged, but are seldom applied in regional modeling. Here, we incorporate one such data set, U‐Surf, into the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, modifying it for WRF's multi‐layer UCM and releasing it as U‐Surf‐WRF. Considering 13 US cities, U‐Surf‐WRF parameters vary more between LCZs than default WRF parameters, with consistently lower impervious fraction. To determine the effects of using U‐Surf‐WRF, we conduct high‐resolution WRF summertime seasonal and recent heatwave simulations for these 13 cities using default and U‐Surf‐WRF parameters. Either prescribed by LCZ or for each grid point, using U‐Surf‐WRF usually yields more accurate surface temperatures. It generally decreases modeled urban air temperature and increases modeled urban humidity, yielding lower heat and dry islands. Decomposing the impact of each U‐Surf‐WRF variable, we find that while albedo can impact daytime simulations, especially for air temperature, morphology and impervious fraction are most relevant, especially for surface temperature. This study demonstrates the impact of city‐specific, facet‐level urban properties in urban‐resolving numerical weather simulations, with remaining gaps against observations demonstrating other challenges in representing cities in process‐based models. Conversely, in WRF simulations with poorly constrained parameters, we suggest caution interpreting the magnitude and spatial distribution of urban signals.

articles.title: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.titleEn: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.abstract: The Congo Basin in Central Africa remains one of the few regions globally where the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has neither assessed changes in hot extremes and extreme precipitation since the 1950s nor attributed such changes to anthropogenic influences, primarily due to the sparsity of in situ observational data. Although extensive daily weather records exist, spanning from the 1900s to the early 2000s and covering numerous stations across the basin, the majority of these remain archived on paper, limiting their accessibility for climate analysis. Here we present and analyse over 1 million temperature and precipitation observations from 37 weather stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have until now been unavailable to the research community. To produce this dataset, we first digitized (imaged) 9885 paper sheets stored in local archives during two dedicated field campaigns. We subsequently apply an improved version of the MeteoSaver software (version 1.1) to transcribe the imaged sheets, yielding daily time series of maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, as well as dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures measured at three times per day (06:00, 15:00, and 18:00 local time). After quality control, analysis of multi-decadal temperature data across the basin reveals a consistent and accelerating warming signal since the 1960s, characterized by a warming shift in the distribution of daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures with each successive decade. Median trends across 21 of the 37 stations with sufficient data availability are 0.22, 0.10, and 0.15 °C per decade for daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, respectively, corresponding to approximately 0.7, 0.3, and 0.5 °C of warming during the 1961–1990 period. We further find an increasing frequency of hot extremes and a decreasing frequency of cold extremes with each successive decade, with the most recent decade exhibiting nearly twice as many hot days per year and fewer cold days compared to the earliest decade. Analysis of precipitation at three stations with sufficient data indicates an increased frequency of heavy precipitation events at two stations and no substantial change at the third; however, limited spatial coverage due to data availability restricts broader conclusions for the DRC. Overall, this analysis of rescued weather data from Central Africa highlights the urgent need to close the knowledge gap on climate trends in the Congo Basin, one of the world's most data-sparse yet climatically significant regions.

articles.title: The OpenSat4Weather dataset: Ku-band satellite link data for precipitation monitoring
articles.titleEn: The OpenSat4Weather dataset: Ku-band satellite link data for precipitation monitoring
articles.abstract: The TV-SAT signals received by the ground antennas of Satellite Microwave Links (SMLs) can be opportunistically used for detecting and quantifying precipitation. Consequently, SMLs have the potential to serve as low-cost rainfall sensors complementing conventional instruments. However, a major challenge for opportunistic sensors, including both SMLs and their terrestrial counterpart – Commercial Microwave Links (CMLs) – is related to data ownership and accessibility constraints, possibly hindering progress in the development of processing tools and validation studies. This limitation highlights the importance of openly accessible datasets. While CML open datasets are already available, there are no large-scale SML datasets in public repositories. To address this gap, we introduce the OpenSat4Weather dataset, a comprehensive and openly accessible collection of measurements from 215 SML sensors deployed in Southern France, over a five-month period from August to December 2022. The dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16530166 (Nebuloni et al., 2025b). OpenSat4Weather also includes concurrent conventional measurements, namely, 6 min rainfall depths from 113 operational rain gauges, and radar-based estimates of rainfall intensity along each SML path. The radar data were derived from the gauge-adjusted weather radar product PANTHERE provided by Météo-France. Additionally, the dataset stores ERA5 reanalysis data of the 0 °C isotherm height for rain height estimation, which are essential for accurately converting the received signal level into rainfall intensity. In this paper, we detail the OpenSat4Weather data preparation process and draw statistics of data availability. We then provide a descriptive analysis of the dataset, including rainfall characteristics, derived from rain gauges, statistical properties of the SML received signal levels, and a comparison between SML and radar data. In addition, we illustrate examples of disturbances and anomalous patterns observed in raw SML signals. Finally, we provide some practical guidelines for processing and analyzing SML data. Our ultimate goal is to promote open research initiatives aimed at accelerating the development of SML-based applications. Enhancing rainfall monitoring by opportunistic sensors has the potential to provide substantial benefits, particularly in regions where conventional networks are sparse or unavailable.

articles.title: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.titleEn: Phenological Flexibility in Nesting Grassland Birds Over a Half Century Informs Timing of Management
articles.abstract: The timing of biological events for wildlife species reflects and influences ecological and evolutionary processes and helps guide management actions to meet conservation objectives. Climate change may cause phenological shifts across trophic levels and ecosystems, which can have broad ecological impacts. Shifts may also result in mistiming between management practices based on historical conditions and current biological events, reducing the effectiveness of natural resource management and conservation efforts. We analyzed nesting phenology patterns over recent decades across North America for 44 species of grassland‐nesting birds, including waterfowl, upland gamebirds, shorebirds, and passerines, many of which have experienced precipitous population declines. Understanding nesting phenologies of these species is important to their conservation, as grassland management activities often conflict with reproductive periods leading to high nest and young mortality. We compiled a dataset of over 172,000 nest records spanning five decades and evaluated environmental factors influencing long‐term shifts and short‐term flexibility in nesting phenology. We found considerable variation in responses among species, with differences in both direction and magnitude of spatiotemporal effects on nest initiation dates. Notably, the community‐level nesting season lengthened over time, but shifts exhibited spatial heterogeneity within this community of grassland birds. Nesting dates shifted asymmetrically across the breeding season with differential changes in early, peak, and late nesting dates whereas long‐term changes were mediated by weather and geographic gradients. For example, nest initiation was earlier in warmer and wetter years. By applying a quantile‐based analysis, we provide estimates of the full nesting period that could serve as a flexible tool for scheduling monitoring efforts and balancing management and human activities with periods of reduced nesting activity. Our collaborative effort illustrates the challenges and opportunities of collecting long‐term data on avian communities necessary for answering questions across large regions but highlights the value of research coordination for bird conservation.

articles.title: What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
articles.titleEn: What matters when? Temporal development of drivers and sources of nitrous oxide emissions in winter wheat
articles.abstract: Agriculture is the largest anthropogenic source of nitrous oxide (N 2 O), primarily due to nitrogen (N) fertilization. Understanding how the influence of key drivers and the relative contribution of source processes change throughout cropping seasons is crucial for developing effective strategies to mitigate N 2 O emissions. In this study, we combined high-resolution eddy covariance (EC) flux measurements and explainable machine learning (ML) across the 2022–2023 winter wheat season and the subsequent summer cover crop at a temperate site in Switzerland, complemented by stable isotope analyses conducted in March 2023 following a fertilization event. We used Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to interpret an XGBoost model trained to predict N 2 O fluxes, enabling a time-resolved assessment of driver contributions. Crop establishment and early spring emerged as particularly vulnerable periods, characterized by mismatches between N supply and plant demand that led to surplus soil mineral N and elevated N 2 O fluxes under favorable moisture and temperature conditions. Elevated gross primary productivity (GPP, used as a proxy for crop activity and N demand) showed a consistent negative effect on N 2 O fluxes, supporting the role of active vegetation as a competing N sink. Stable isotope source partitioning identified denitrification as the dominant N 2 O production pathway during the early-spring post-fertilization period, consistent with poor soil drainage and high soil moisture. Cumulative N 2 O emissions over the nine-month winter wheat season reached 5.5 kg N 2 O-N ha −1 , with yield-scaled emissions of 1.1 kg N 2 O-N Mg −1 grain, both values exceeding those typically reported for wheat. Our findings highlight the value of combining EC, explainable ML, and stable isotope approaches to resolve the temporal dynamics of N 2 O emissions and identify vulnerable windows for targeted mitigation in cropping systems.

articles.title: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
articles.titleEn: Linking marine benthic biodiversity and ecosystem functions related to carbon cycling in a continental mud depocenter
articles.abstract: The importance of carbon storage in continental seafloor sediments is increasingly recognized, yet the role of benthic macrofaunal biodiversity in the regulation of these processes remains poorly understood. Benthic macrofauna contributes to organic carbon cycling through respiration and secondary production, while sediment reworking (bioturbation) and ventilation (bioirrigation) by infauna promote the redistribution and remineralization of organic matter in sediments. Here, we investigated how benthic community structure, functional traits, and the relationship between biodiversity and calculated potential ecosystem functioning related to carbon cycling vary along environmental gradients in muddy sediments of the southeastern North Sea. Based on 171 macrofaunal taxa collected from 50 stations, hierarchical clustering based on abundance data categorized the macrofaunal communities into four distinct structural groups. Distance-based redundancy analysis (dbRDA) revealed that community functional composition was primarily structured by bottom hydrodynamics (salinity and bottom shear stress) and sediment characteristics (sorting, skewness, kurtosis, and D50). Biomass-weighted functional trait vectors, mapped onto a non-metric multidimensional scaling (nMDS) space, showed a clear structural shift with communities in the deep clusters being dominated by mobile biodiffusors and subsurface filter feeders, whereas shallow clusters were characterized by less mobile, surface-modifying bivalves and polychaetes. These contrasting patterns led to pronounced differences in calculated potential ecosystem functioning: bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were significantly higher in deeper communities, whereas the calculated community secondary production and respiration were higher in shallow communities. Across all stations, community secondary production and respiration increased with taxonomic and functional richness, while bioturbation and bioirrigation potentials were negatively related to biodiversity and community evenness. Interaction regressions and simple slope analyses revealed that environmental gradients significantly modulated the biodiversity–ecosystem functioning (BEF) relationships. Our findings demonstrate that environmental gradients fundamentally shape both benthic community structure and the link between biodiversity and essential ecosystem functions related to carbon dynamics in fine-grained sediment and organic matter in shelf sea systems.

articles.title: Human-centred design approaches to tsunami mitigation under sea level rise in Kesennuma, Japan
articles.titleEn: Human-centred design approaches to tsunami mitigation under sea level rise in Kesennuma, Japan
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Human-centred design (HCD) is increasingly prioritised as studies show human experience is critical in infrastructure use, and recent policies call for more socially responsive design. Tsunami impacts intensify as sea level rise (SLR) raises baseline water levels and reduces existing defence effectiveness. This study aims to develop and evaluate HCD-integrated multi-layered tsunami defences, assessing whether socially integrated designs can deliver effective protection under projected SLR conditions. Based on identified infrastructure preferences in Kesennuma City, Japan, we develop three multi-layered defence configurations: an environmentally integrated eco-hybrid system (Defence 1), a discreet open-feeling barrier system (Defence 2), and a reinforced high-performance system (Defence 3). Using TUNAMI-N2 numerical modelling, 150 simulations combine three tsunami sources, five SLR conditions, and five defence states. Results for inundation extent, fatality rates, and economic loss show a consistent hierarchy: Defence 3 achieves the strongest containment, while Defence 2, which more closely aligns with residents' preferences for openness and access, delivers near equivalent reductions typically within 10 %–15 %. Defence 1 provides only limited hazard reduction and is unsuitable as a standalone mitigation system. We show that HCD-integrated configurations can deliver strong technical performance and support a shift toward socially integrated, multi-layered tsunami protection under rising sea levels.

articles.title: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.titleEn: A Catchment‐Based Global Model of River Discharge and Flow Velocity for Earth System Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The representation of river flows in Earth System Models (ESMs) is crucial for understanding water resources availability, contaminant transport, and the impacts of climate change on river systems. In this study, we introduce a global runoff routing model founded on hydraulic geometry principles and hydrologic catchments, specifically designed for integration with ESMs. To simulate river dynamics, the model capitalizes on (a) the river network topology defined by the Pfafstetter coding system, (b) hydraulic geometry principles that connect river discharge to flow velocity, and (c) calibration using more than 2.7 million intermittent field measurements of flow velocity in the contiguous US (CONUS). The model is shown to produce reasonably accurate natural daily river discharge over CONUS except within some arid regions and the region adjacent to the Great Lakes, where streamflow is strongly impacted by reservoir management and by the natural buffering behavior of the large lakes themselves. The average correlation coefficient for discharge (vs. in situ measurements) is 0.80 for tested major rivers over CONUS except in arid regions and the Great Lakes. A unique feature of the model is its ability to simulate flow velocity with realistic magnitudes, standing it in good stead for tracer tracking and water management applications.

articles.title: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.titleEn: An Online Moisture Tagging Framework for Detrainment of Convective Hydrometeors and Associated Precipitation in Convection‐Permitting Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Convective detrainment is an important process in mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) that strongly influence adjacent stratiform clouds and precipitation. However, it remains difficult to quantify convective detrainment in numerical models. In this study, we develop an online convection identification and water vapor tracer (WVT) framework based on the Eulerian WVTs coupled with Weather Research and Forecasting convection‐permitting model. Convection is identified using radar reflectivity, and two types of tracers are introduced to track water species and precipitation within convective regions and those detrained from them, which can be distinguished from those newly generated in the stratiform areas. The framework is applied to both an idealized case and a real case. In the idealized simulation, the framework captures the convective detrainment and its associated precipitation during the lifecycle of convective systems featured by rapid evolution in location and structure. In the real case, the framework demonstrates distinct temporal variations in the intensity and area coverage of stratiform precipitation produced by convective detrainment. Both the ice‐ and liquid‐phase detrainments decrease dramatically at the moment when convective precipitation starts to increase, suggesting intensified conversion from cloud to precipitating hydrometeors. After that, the conversion efficiency weakens, which is favorable for the formation of stratiform clouds and precipitation. Overall, this framework provides a useful tool for quantifying the characteristics and impacts of convective detrainment and for evaluating convective parameterization schemes.

In the real case, the framework demonstrates distinct temporal variations in the intensity and area coverage of stratiform precipitation produced by convective detrainment. Both the ice‐ and liquid‐phase detrainments decrease dramatically at the moment when convective precipitation starts to increase, suggesting intensified conversion from cloud to precipitating hydrometeors. After that, the conversion efficiency weakens, which is favorable for the formation of stratiform clouds and precipitation. Overall, this framework provides a useful tool for quantifying the characteristics and impacts of convective detrainment and for evaluating convective parameterization schemes.

articles.title: The influence of lakes and reservoirs on estimated flood peaks at hourly vs. daily timescale in the Alps
articles.titleEn: The influence of lakes and reservoirs on estimated flood peaks at hourly vs. daily timescale in the Alps
articles.abstract: Water bodies such as lakes and reservoirs can play a crucial role in reducing estimated flood peaks, at both daily and hourly time resolution. While the effect of water bodies on flood peaks has been demonstrated in the past at different time resolutions, it remains unclear how water bodies affect the ratio between estimated daily and hourly quantiles, that is, to which degree their attenuation effect is scale dependent. Here, we analyse how water bodies influence this ratio using two approaches: (1) by comparing estimated daily and hourly flood peak quantiles upstream and downstream of reservoirs of four local case studies, and (2) by comparing daily and hourly flood peak quantiles across a large sample of catchments in Switzerland with various degrees of water-body influence. Our results show that reservoirs dampen hourly peak discharge much more strongly than daily peak discharge, which leads to similar daily and hourly flood peaks downstream of reservoirs. Specifically, our case study analysis highlights that (sub-)hourly peak discharge is attenuated by up to 70 % downstream of reservoirs during flood events with a 10-year return period. We also find that the attenuation effect is particularly pronounced in catchments that are heavily influenced by water bodies, i.e. those catchments where more than 60 % of the area contributes to water body inflow. This implies that daily flood peaks are a good proxy for hourly peaks in strongly regulated catchments in contrast to natural ones. We conclude that considering water body influence on flood peaks is crucial to understand the similarity between daily and hourly flood peaks downstream of water bodies. This suggests that water body influence should also be considered in large-sample studies for which the exact influence may be unknown, and quantified using suitable metrics such as the fraction of the total catchment above the water body.

articles.title: The influence of vapor pressure deficit changes on global terrestrial evapotranspiration
articles.titleEn: The influence of vapor pressure deficit changes on global terrestrial evapotranspiration
articles.abstract: Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) has been widely recognized as a key driver of uncertainty in future global evapotranspiration ( E ) trends. Accurately characterizing the spatiotemporal dynamics of VPD and elucidating its influence on terrestrial E are critical for understanding land–atmosphere water and energy feedback processes under climate warming. However, previous studies have largely focused on the physiological regulation of plant transpiration ( E t ) at the leaf or canopy scale, leaving the quantitative understanding of VPD– E interactions at the global scale incomplete. By integrating multi-source remote sensing products and reanalysis datasets, this study quantitatively evaluates the role of VPD in regulating global terrestrial E variability. The main findings are as follows: (1) Approximately 60.7 % of global land area exhibits positive apparent sensitivity of E to VPD, with a global mean sensitivity of 293.3±62.3 mm hPa −1 , and stronger responses observed in warm and humid regions. (2) VPD is positively correlated with E t overall, particularly in mid-to-high latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere, whereas its correlation with bare soil evaporation ( E b ) is weaker and tends to be negative in water-limited regions. (3) The VPD– E relationship exhibits a pronounced aridity-dependent threshold, which decreases progressively from arid (1.90 kPa) and semi-arid (1.46 kPa) regions to semi-humid (0.49 kPa) and humid (0.47 kPa) regions. Further path analysis reveals that VPD regulates E through interconnected pathways involving atmospheric demand, soil moisture, vegetation physiology, and energy supply, with an overall negative net effect on E . This study clarifies the dominant pathways and regional heterogeneity of VPD– E interactions at the global scale, providing quantitative constraints for predicting the response of the terrestrial water cycle to increasing atmospheric aridity.
